questions.question: Which Articles of the Indian Constitution describe Fundamental Rights?
questions.solution:
The Correct Answer is **Articles 12 to 35.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The** Fundamental Rights** are enshrined in **Part III of the Constitution (Articles 12-35).**
 
• **Part III of the Constitution** is described as the **Magna Carta of India.**
 
• **‘Magna Carta’**, the Charter of Rights issued by King John of England in 1215 was the first written document relating to the Fundamental Rights of citizens.
 
• The Fundamental Rights: The Constitution of India provides for six Fundamental Rights:
 
 
• **Right to equality (Articles 14–18)**
 
• **Right to freedom (Articles 19–22)**
 
• **Right against exploitation (Articles 23–24)**
 
• **Right to freedom of religion (Articles 25–28)**
 
• **Cultural and educational rights (Articles 29–30)**
 
• **Right to constitutional remedies (Article 32)**
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Originally the constitution also included Right to property (Article 31).**
 
• However, it was deleted from the list of **Fundamental Rights by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978.**
 
• It is made a** legal right under Article 300-A in Part XII of the Constitution.**
 
• **Provision for Laws Violating Fundamental Rights**:
 
 
• Article 13 of the Indian constitution declares that all laws that are inconsistent with or in derogation of any of the fundamental rights shall be void.
 
 
 
• This power has been conferred on the Supreme Court (Article 32) and the high courts **(Article 226).**
 
• Further, the article declares that a constitutional amendment cannot be challenged (as it is not a law).
 
• However, the **Supreme Court in the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973)** held that a Constitutional amendment can be challenged if it violates a fundamental right.

__
 
• **Republic Day****​**

 
 
• **Republic Day is celebrated every year on the 26th of January**.
 
• It marks the day when the Constitution of India came into effect in 1950, **replacing the Government of India Act (1935)** as the governing document of India.
 
• On this day, India officially became a sovereign, democratic republic, and its people chose their government.
 
• The Republic Day celebration in India is a grand event with various ceremonial parades, cultural performances, and the iconic Republic Day parade held at Rajpath in New Delhi.
 
• **The President of India hoists the national flag**, and various achievements of the nation are showcased during the celebrations.
 
• The Presiden takes the salute during the Republic Day parade at New Delhi.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• Historical Background: India gained independence from British colonial rule on August 15, 1947. However, it was on January 26, 1950, that India adopted its Constitution, becoming a fully sovereign and democratic republic.
 
• Adoption of the Constitution: The Constituent Assembly of India, under the leadership of Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, worked diligently to draft the Constitution of India, which took almost three years to complete.
 
 
• The Constitution was adopted on November 26, 1949, and came into effect on January 26, 1950.
 
 
 
• Purna Swaraj Declaration: Interestingly, January 26 has a historical significance even before the adoption of the Constitution.
 
 
• On January 26, 1930, the Indian National Congress declared the "Purna Swaraj" (Complete Independence) resolution, marking the demand for complete self-rule and freedom from British rule.
 
 
 
• **Republic Day Celebrations**: The Republic Day celebrations in India are marked by various events, with the main parade held in the national capital, New Delhi. The President of India takes the salute at the Republic Day parade, which showcases the country's military might, cultural diversity, achievements, and socio-economic progress.
 
• Chief Guest: Each year, a **foreign head of state or a dignitary **is invited as the chief guest for the Republic Day parade.
 
 
• This tradition symbolizes **India's diplomatic ties and global friendships**.
 
 
 
• Flag Hoisting and Celebrations: Republic Day is celebrated throughout the country with enthusiasm and patriotic fervour. 
 
 
• The national flag is hoisted in **schools, government offices, and public places**.
 
• Cultural programs flag hoisting ceremonies, and parades are organized in various cities and towns.
 
 
 
• **Importance of the Constitution**
 
 
• ​Republic Day not only commemorates the adoption of the Constitution but also emphasizes the significance of the guiding principles and fundamental rights enshrined in it.
 
• The Constitution of India serves as the supreme law of the country, ensuring justice, liberty, equality, and fraternity for all citizens.

questions.question: According to the Koppen classification,Which regions experience cold humid winter with short summers?
questions.solution:

Koeppen based his scheme of climatic classification on monthly values of temperature and precipitation.

 
• He identified five major climatic types, namely:
 
 
• Tropical climates, where the mean monthly temperature throughout the year is over 18°C.
 
• Dry climates, where precipitation is very low in comparison to temperature, and hence, dry. If dryness is less, it is semiarid (S); if it is more, the climate is arid(W).
 
• Warm temperate climates, where the mean temperature of the coldest month is between 18°C and minus 3°C.
 
• Cool temperate climates, where the mean temperature of the warmest month is over 10°C, and the mean temperature of the coldest month is under minus 3°C.
 
• Ice climates, where the mean temperature of the warmest month is under 10°C.
 
 

Major climatic types of India based on Koeppen’s scheme have been described below: ​

• ​The Brahmaputra, one of the largest rivers in the world, has its origin in the Chemayungdung glacier of the Kailash range near the Mansarovar lake.

• The Rango Tsangpo is the major right-bank tributary of this river in Tibet. It emerges as a turbulent and dynamic river after carving out a deep gorge in the Central Himalayas near Namcha Barwa (7,755 m).
 
• The river emerges from the foothills under the name of Siang or Dihang.
 
 
 
• It enters India from Arunachal Pradesh.
 
 
• Flowing southwest, it receives its main left-bank tributaries, viz., Dibang or Sikang and Lohit, thereafter, it is known as the Brahmaputra.
 
 
 
• The Brahmaputra receives numerous tributaries in its 750 km long journey through the Assam valley.
 
 
• Its major left bank tributaries are the Burhi Dihing and Dhansari (South) whereas the important right bank tributaries are the Subansiri, Kameng, Manas and Sankosh. The Subansiri which has its origin in Tibet, is an antecedent river.
 
 
 
• The Brahmaputra enters Bangladesh near Dhubri and flows southward.
 
 
• In Bangladesh, the Tista joins it on its right bank from where the river is known as the Jamuna.
 
• It finally merges with the river Padma, which falls in the Bay of Bengal.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

**Bindusara - **

• He was a Greek Amitrochates (b.c 320 BCE—died 272/3 BCE).
 
• According to Greek historians, he was known as Amitrochates, which is derived from the Sanskrit word amitraghata, which means “destroyer of opponents.”

**Dasharatha - **

 
• Dasaratha Maurya, grandson of Ashoka the Great, ruled as the fourth emperor of the Mauryan Empire from 232 BCE to 224 BCE. Here's a detailed breakdown of his reign:
 
• **Background:**
 
 
• Ascended the throne after his grandfather, Ashoka.
 
• Unlike Ashoka, who was known for his military conquests before embracing Buddhism, Dasaratha's reign is associated with the decline of the Mauryan Empire.
 
 
 
• **Challenges during his reign:**
 
 
• Loss of Territories: Several regions of the vast Mauryan Empire declared independence during Dasaratha's rule. This weakened the empire's central authority.
 
• Limited Ability: Historians believe Dasaratha may not have possessed the strong leadership qualities needed to hold the empire together.
 
 
 
• **Positive aspects:**
 
 
• Continued Ashoka's Policies: Dasaratha is known for upholding the social and religious policies established by his grandfather, particularly the promotion of Dharma (righteousness) and non-violence.
 
• Patronage of Ajivikas: Inscriptions in the Barabar Caves suggest Dasaratha may have patronized the Ajivika sect, a non-vedic philosophical tradition that existed alongside Buddhism during that period.
 
 
 
• **Legacy:**
 
 
• Dasaratha's reign is considered a turning point in Mauryan history. The decline of the empire that began under him continued in the following years.
 
• He was the last Mauryan emperor to leave behind epigraphical evidence (inscriptions) of his rule.
 
• Dasaratha's successor was his cousin, Samprati, who attempted to revive the empire.
 
 
 
• **Ashoka - **
 
 
• Ashoka the Great (r. 268-232 BCE) was the third king of the Mauryan Empire (322-185 BCE)
 
• He is best known for his renunciation of war, development of the concept of dhamma (pious social conduct), and promotion of Buddhism as well as his effective reign of a nearly pan-Indian political entity.

questions.question:
Choose the correct statement(s) related to ‘continentality’.

a. The sea exerts a moderating influence on climate.

b. As the distance from the sea increases, the people experience extreme weather conditions.

c. As one goes from the surface of the earth to higher altitudes, the atmosphere becomes less dense and temperature decreases.
questions.solution:
**The correct answer is: A and B only**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** 

 

__
 
• **The sea exerts a moderating influence on climate:**

 
 
• This statement is **correct**.
 
• Large bodies of water, such as seas and oceans, have a high capacity for heat storage and release. This results in a moderating effect on the climate of coastal areas, leading to milder winters and cooler summers.
 
• For example, London (close to the Atlantic Ocean) has a more moderate climate compared to Moscow, which is further inland.
 
 
 
• **As the distance from the sea increases, the people experience extreme weather conditions:**
 
 
• This statement is **correct**.
 
• Continental regions, which are far from the sea, often experience more extreme temperature variations. This is because they lack the moderating influence of the ocean, resulting in hotter summers and colder winters.
 
• For example, areas like Siberia (inland Russia) and Central Canada exhibit extreme temperatures due to their distance from the moderating effects of large water bodies.
 
 
 
• **As one goes from the surface of the earth to higher altitudes, the atmosphere becomes less dense and temperature decreases:**
 
 
• This statement is **incorrect**.
 
• Although this statement is true in a general sense (i.e., atmospheric density decreases with altitude and temperatures drop in a typical troposphere), it is not directly related to the concept of 'continentality', which deals specifically with distance from large water bodies.
 
• This concept is more relevant to the study of vertical climate zones and phenomena like the adiabatic lapse rate.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Continentality:**

 
 
• Continentality refers to the climatic condition of areas located far from the influence of the ocean, leading to greater temperature extremes.
 
• Land heats up and cools down more quickly than water, which is why inland areas experience more significant temperature variations compared to coastal areas.
 
 
 
• **Moderating Influence of the Sea:**
 
 
• The ocean's ability to store and release large amounts of heat moderates the climate of coastal regions.
 
• This effect can reduce the severity of temperature extremes, leading to more stable and mild climates in areas close to large bodies of water.
 
 
 
• **Impact of Altitude on Climate:**
 
 
• While altitude does indeed affect temperature and atmospheric density, it is a separate concept from continentality.
 
• Higher altitudes generally experience cooler temperatures and thinner air compared to sea level, which is a factor considered in vertical climate zonation.

questions.question: The Arms Act was passed in _____ that prevented Indians from keeping arms without an appropriate license.
questions.solution:
The Correct Answer is __**1878**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The Arms Act**

 
 
• Between 1876 and 1880, Lord Lytton held the position of Viceroy of India.
 
• He approved both the 1878** Arms Act** and the Vernacular Press** Act.**
 
• The** Arms** Act was developed by the British during the 19th century in response to the rising Indian nationalism.
 
• It became law in 1878.
 
• The production and sale of fir**earms** in the nation were controlled by this statute.
 
• No Indian was permitted to produce, market, or even possess a weapon without first obtaining a government permission.
 
• The British intended to prevent Indians from possessing rifles and pistols because they did not want another uprising like the one that occurred in 1857 CE.
 
• The act underwent significant amendments in **1959 and 1983**, but there was no specific amendment that disallowed Indians from possessing arms.
 
• However, in **1962**, the Indian government passed the Defence of India Rules, which prohibited the possession of arms and ammunition by any person without a valid license.
 
• **This law was enacted during the Indo-China** War to prevent unauthorized persons from possessing arms that could be used against the country's interests.
 
• In **1983**, the Arms Act was amended to further regulate the **possession of firearms and ammunition in the country**.
 
• The amendment tightened the licensing requirements and imposed stricter penalties for** violations of the law.****​**
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Lord Litton****​**

 
 
• Edward Robert Lytton Bulwer-Lytton, 1st Earl of Lytton, also known as Lord Lytton, was an English politician who was Viceroy of India from 1876 to 1880.
 
• The first Famine Commission was set up in 1878 under the Chairmanship of Sir Richard Strachey. The commission recommended state interference in food trade in the event of famine. India witnessed another major famine in 1896-97.
 
• Lytton's viceroyalty was characterized by ruthlessness in both domestic and foreign affairs.
 
• At the time, India was in the grip of a famine caused by crop failure in 1876. In response, he called a **Durbar and declared Queen Victoria to be the "Empress of India".**
 
• Vernacular Press Act**(1878**)​
 
 
• People were dissatisfied with Lytton's unpopular policies, and the native vernacular press mocked him. He drafted the Vernacular Press Act to curtail the wings of the Vernacular Press.
 
• By virtue of this act, District Magistrates were empowered, without prior permission from the government, to compel a printer and publisher of any kind to enter into a bond, undertaking not to publish anything that might incite discontent against the government.
 
• The magistrate was also given the authority to deposit security, which could be confiscated if the printer violated the bond.
 
• If the printer violates this again, his press may be seized.
 
• The worst aspect of this Act was that it discriminated against Native Vernacular Press and loyal Anglo-Indian Press and was dubbed the Gagging Act.
 
• It was specifically aimed at Amrita Bazaar Patrika, which had turned English overnight in order to avoid being caught up in the act.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Resorcinol, also known as** m-dihydroxybenzene,** with the molecular formula C6H4(OH)2**.**
 
• It is an isomer of** benzenediol.**
 
• The name “**resorcinol**” is derived from the Latin word** “resina,” **which means** resin.**
 
• Resorcinol appears as **white to light pink crystals** or a powder. It is **odorless**. It is soluble in **water, alcohol, and ether.**
 
• Resorcinol is commonly used in topical medications for** treating skin conditions** such as** acne, psoriasis, and eczema.**
 
• It acts as a** keratolytic agent,** helping to remove** dead skin cells.**

**​ ** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

**m-Cresol:**

 
• m-Cresol is a **colorless liquid,** with the molecular formula **C₇H₈O.**
 
• It has a strong, **sweet odor.**
 
• It is used in the production of** resins, disinfectants, and synthetic fragrances.**

**Catechol:**

 
• Catechol is a** white crystalline solid**, with the molecular formula** C₆H₄(OH)₂**
 
• It is used in** photography**, as a reducing agent, and in the synthesis of pharmaceuticals.
 
• Catechol is the** 1,2-isomer of benzenediol.**

**​Glycerol:**

 
• Glycerol is a thick, **colorless liquid,** with the molecular formula **C₃H₈O₃**
 
• It is commonly used in **cosmetics, food, and pharmaceuticals**. It is a component of **fats and oils**.
